type: legislative gap (timeline delegated to unissued regulation)
title: No statutory clock for notifying a breach of children's data
finding: PDPL Art. 9 requires the controller to notify the UAE Data Office and the data subject of a breach, but only 'within the period ... set by the Executive Regulations'. Art. 28 required those Regulations within six months of the law; legal trackers report they were still unpublished in October 2026, so neither the operator nor the school nor the guardian knows the deadline, and Art. 26 penalties also wait for a Cabinet decision.
uae_evidence: notify the Bureau of such breach
within six \(6\) months as of the date on which the Decree by Law is promulgated
global_note: EU AI Act Art. 73 fixes the report window for serious incidents involving high-risk AI (immediately after the causal link is established and no later than 15 days; shorter for widespread infringements). The OECD AI Principles ask for traceability so incidents can be analysed.
recommendation: Issue the PDPL Executive Regulations with a fixed notification window, and a shorter one where the data subjects are children; until then, the Data Office could publish interim guidance that education providers notify within a stated number of hours.

title: Education platforms may be exempted from the under-13 data rule by a resolution that does not exist yet
finding: Decree-Law 26/2025 Art. 7(1) bars platforms from processing under-13s' data without explicit, documented, verifiable parental consent, but Art. 7(3) lets platforms 'used for educational or health purposes' be exempted by a Cabinet Resolution 'provided that the necessary measures are taken'. The criteria, the approving body's process and the substitute safeguards are not in the KB, so an AI tutor cannot tell which regime applies to a 12-year-old who slipped through an age gate.
uae_evidence: educational or health purposes shall be exempted
under the age of thirteen \(13\), unless
global_examples: obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection
Definition and enforcement of age limit
global_note: COPPA (16 CFR 312.5) requires verifiable parental consent before any collection from under-13s and lists accepted verification methods; UNESCO's GenAI guidance asks governments to define and enforce an age limit (it suggests 13) for GenAI use in education.
recommendation: Publish the Art. 7(3) resolution with explicit criteria for 'educational platform', the safeguards that replace parental consent (e.g. school authorisation plus parent notice), and a public register of exempted platforms.

title: Teenagers' consent is not addressed by the PDPL
finding: The PDPL contains no provision on children or on the age at which a person can consent (a full-text search of the KB copy finds no 'child' or 'minor'), and Decree-Law 26/2025 sets the parental-consent rule only for under-13s although it defines a child as under 18. For 13-17-year-olds using an AI tutor, whether the student, the parent or the school's enrolment contract supplies valid consent is left to interpretation, which is exactly the dispute in the unverified-consent scenario.
uae_evidence: Child : Any human being who has not completed the age of eighteen
global_examples: Age appropriate application: Take a risk-based
global_note: The UK Children's Code applies to all under-18s, with standards by age band (best interests, DPIA, age-appropriate application, high-privacy defaults, no detrimental use of data); UNICEF's Guidance on AI and Children 3.0 asks states to give schools guidance on procuring and deploying AI.
recommendation: Define in PDPL Executive Regulations (or a Data Office code) how consent works for 13-17-year-olds and whether a school enrolment clause can serve as the basis for third-party AI tools; an age-banded design code modelled on the UK Children's Code would cover the rest.

title: The same AI tutor falls under different data-protection regimes depending on who deploys it
finding: PDPL Art. 2(2) excludes government data and 'governmental entities which control or process Personal Data', and companies in free zones with their own data-protection law. A tool used in a public (government) school, a Dubai private school and a free-zone EdTech company could therefore sit under three different rule-sets for the same student data.
global_note: The EU AI Act classifies education AI by use (Annex III point 3: admission, evaluating learning outcomes, steering learning, monitoring tests) and applies whether the deployer is public or private.
recommendation: Give education AI a use-based rule that applies to public and private deployers alike (for example through MoE/KHDA procurement conditions or the Child Digital Safety platform classification under Art. 6).

title: No binding risk class, logging duty or incident channel for AI systems used with students
finding: UAE AI governance documents in the KB (AI Charter 2024, AI Ethics Principles and Guidelines 2022, Dubai AI Ethics Guidelines) are principles; the Ethics Guidelines state they are non-binding. None defines when an education AI system is high-risk, what it must log, who must oversee it, or where an AI incident (such as harmful advice to a 14-year-old after a silent model swap) is reported.
global_note: EU AI Act: education uses listed as high-risk (Annex III point 3), automatic event logging (Art. 12), human oversight (Art. 14), accuracy/robustness (Art. 15), serious-incident reporting (Art. 73).
recommendation: Adopt an education-AI conformity baseline (risk class, event logging, human oversight, change notification when the underlying model changes, incident reporting) that KHDA/MoE can require in procurement; ITU-T Y.3172's sandbox and policy node are a natural technical reference.

type: unclear responsibility (rules exist for some schools only)
title: Approved-tool and age rules cover MoE-curriculum schools; Dubai private schools on other curricula wait for KHDA
finding: The MoE National AI Literacy Curriculum Framework refers to a Guide that defines approved tools, permissible classroom use and age restrictions for Grades 7-12 in public schools and private schools following the MoE curriculum. Private schools on British, Indian, IB or American curricula are outside that Guide; KHDA's own AI guidance for Dubai private schools was announced in October 2026 for next year (press reports), and the KB holds only one KHDA line on AI (teachers must not use AI to replace human judgement on student matters).
global_note: UNESCO asks institutions to validate GenAI tools for ethical and pedagogical fit before use; UNICEF asks governments to give schools procurement and deployment guidance.
recommendation: KHDA guidance should state which tools are approved, the age bands, and how a school checks a third-party AI tutor; a shared MoE-KHDA register would avoid two lists.

title: Exam contingency rules cover cancelled exam boards, not failing AI services
finding: KHDA's 2026 Examination Contingency guide responds to the cancellation of board examinations across the Middle East in 2026; it does not address an EdTech or AI provider outage during assessments. PDPL Art. 20 asks for measures that ensure timely access to personal data after a technical failure, but nothing sets availability or fallback expectations for AI study tools at exam time.
global_note: OECD AI Principle 1.4: robust, secure and safe throughout the lifecycle, with mechanisms to override, repair or decommission; EU AI Act Art. 15: resilience to errors and faults, technical redundancy and fail-safe plans.
recommendation: Add AI-service continuity to school contingency planning: a degraded, non-AI mode that keeps students' plans and notes available, exam-period change freezes, and provider SLAs.

type: conflict of objectives (cost vs. data residency)
title: Low-cost model access pushes student data across borders on terms schools cannot check
finding: PDPL Art. 22-23 allow transfers abroad to adequate jurisdictions or under contract/consent, with the controls left to the Executive Regulations (Art. 23(2)). Cheap or free hosted models are often served from outside the UAE and some free tiers may retain prompts; during an outage the cheapest fallback can be a foreign region. The National AI Strategy's goal of wide AI adoption and the protection of children's data pull in different directions with no tie-breaker.
global_examples: Detrimental use of data: Do not use
global_note: The UK Children's Code tells services not to use children's data in ways shown to be detrimental to them and to run a DPIA; OECD asks for traceability of datasets and processes.
recommendation: Publish an adequacy list and standard contract clauses for AI model providers, and require education tools to disclose model-provider location and retention terms.

title: Several regulators can claim a children's-data AI incident; none is named lead
finding: In the simulations the Data Office (PDPL), the Child Digital Safety Council / TDRA (Decree-Law 26/2025) and KHDA (school safeguarding) each have a mandate over the same incident and each received different facts at different times. Decree-Law 26/2025 creates the Council to coordinate ministries and federal, local and private bodies, but the KB has no joint incident protocol or single reporting point for education AI.
global_note: The EU AI Act (Art. 70) makes each Member State designate a market surveillance authority as single point of contact for the regulation.
recommendation: A single intake point for AI incidents involving children (one report reaches the Data Office, the Council/TDRA and the education regulator), with a lead-authority rule by incident type.
